A dynamic assembly is a code container built while the program is running. This is a specialised tool; start with a tiny method that simply returns a number.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Build a method in steps

AssemblyBuilder creates a dynamic assembly; DefineDynamicModule creates its module; DefineType creates a type; DefineMethod declares a method. ILGenerator writes CIL instructions. Ldc_I4_7 pushes the integer7 onto the evaluation stack; Ret returns it. CreateType finishes the generated type so reflection can call it.

Expected result and limits

The full downloadable program emits a public static Seven method and prints Emitted result:7. Dynamic assemblies can support proxies, runtime adapters and generated methods. They are not required for ordinary CRUD and do not automatically compile pasted C# source. Reflection.Emit may be unavailable in restricted/AOT environments. Prefer a normal class when the behaviour is known at build time.

Try it yourself

Change the generated method to return 9.

Worked answer

Use il.Emit(OpCodes.Ldc_I4,9) before Ret, keeping the return type int.

Why is loading arbitrary generated code dangerous?

Worked answer

It runs with process permissions. Do not accept untrusted instructions or assemblies as if they were harmless data.
